strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated problem (planning/grounding domain bias in GUI agents) with an appropriate contribution type: an applied/systems framework rather than a new algorithm, and the claims are matched to that type.

The core idea of retrieving and annotating web tutorial videos at test time (rather than from a pre-built corpus) is a meaningful advance over the most related prior work, and the subtitle-driven three-stage Video-RAG pipeline is a sensible, well-motivated design exploiting an underused modality.

Empirical evidence is unusually thorough for this kind of systems paper: full OSWorld benchmark (361 tasks) across three agent architectures, knowledge-channel ablations, grounding element-count ablation, annotator-model ablation, human evaluation of two pipeline stages (classification precision 100%, topic extraction 96% acceptable), and a detailed cost analysis.

The Meaningful-filter evaluation (Appendix D) and per-mode failure analysis (Appendix F, with concrete planning-mismatch and grounding-mismatch cases) show honest self-assessment and go beyond the minimum; the identified failure modes and proposed mitigations are substantive.

Reproducibility support is good: full prompt structures for both integration modes, complete implementation hyperparameters, and token/cost accounting are provided; the approach is training-free and architecture-agnostic, making it easy for others to adopt.

The dual-channel analysis (planning dominates, grounding complementary in UI-complex domains) and the finding that pipeline structure matters more than annotator strength are useful, transferable insights.
weaknesses: A potentially important confound is not fully controlled: the Mode B integration adds a structured 'guided CoT' thought template alongside the retrieved knowledge. It is not entirely clear whether the No-Annotation baseline uses the same template, so part of the reported gain could come from improved scaffolding rather than domain knowledge. A control with the same template but generic/no retrieved content is needed to cleanly attribute the improvement.

The comparison to Watch & Learn is indirect: it is evaluated on a different agent (Jedi) and reports only the overall score, so the '+2.2 vs. +4.47' claim is a rough comparison rather than an apples-to-apples result; the abstract's 'outperforming by a large margin' phrasing overstates what the evidence supports.

Only OSWorld is used for end evaluation, and OSWorld's applications (GIMP, LibreOffice, VLC) are popular with abundant YouTube tutorials; the 82.8% retrieval coverage and gains may not transfer to niche or newly released software where the claimed 'continuous adaptation' advantage would matter most. A second benchmark or a deliberately OOD application subset would strengthen generalization claims.

Heavy dependence on closed-source, non-deterministic components (GPT-5.1, GPT-4.1-mini, Seed-1.8, live YouTube search) weakens reproducibility: retrieved videos and API behaviors change over time, so exact replication is difficult, and the system's cost structure is tied to specific proprietary pricing.

The ablations rest on small subsets (50 tasks; per-domain counts of 1-8 in Tab. 3), so conclusions such as the k=5 optimum (+11.99pp) and per-domain ablation patterns are likely within noise; the paper does not report variance or statistical significance for any result.

Minor inconsistencies: the abstract claims 'over 5%' improvements while the intro/conclusion claim '4.5-7.5%'; planning-only is not reported for the multi-agent AgentS3 configuration, limiting the dual-channel analysis on Mode A; and the paper does not quantify how often injected knowledge actively hurts (the failure section is qualitative only).

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: GUI agents' performance gaps on domain-specific applications, and proposes a training-free, plug-and-play solution that is architecture-agnostic (validated across a single 8B open-source model, a closed-source model, and a multi-agent system).

Comprehensive evaluation on the full OSWorld benchmark (361 tasks) rather than a subset, with consistent gains across three agent architectures and per-domain breakdowns, including execution-step and latency analysis.

Ablations are informative: knowledge-channel ablation (planning dominates, ~86-91% of gain), grounding element count k (clear information-noise trade-off peaking at k=5), and annotator model comparison, which also yields a useful cost-effectiveness analysis.

The human evaluation of pipeline stages (domain classification with 100% precision/91% recall; topic extraction with 96% acceptable rate) and the Meaningful filter study (Sec. D) go beyond typical end-to-end reporting and increase confidence in the pipeline's internal quality.

Transparent failure analysis (Sec. F) with concrete examples of planning and grounding mismatch, and honest reporting of limitations such as network issues affecting Chrome tasks and API anti-distillation artifacts.
Detailed reproducibility-oriented appendices: full prompts, pipeline configuration, and an unusually complete API cost accounting (retrieval ~$0.019/task, annotation ~$0.25/video).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the system is a well-engineered combination of existing components (yt-dlp search, Whisper ASR, OmniParser, LLM/VLM prompting, inverse-dynamics annotation already used by Watch & Learn and VideoAgentTrek). The core deltas over Watch & Learn—live retrieval, subtitle-driven filtering, richer annotation—are incremental and prompt-level rather than algorithmic.

The critical missing control: no ablation injects irrelevant or generic knowledge of comparable length through the same CoT prompt structure. Since planning knowledge accounts for most of the gain and is delivered via a heavily scaffolded guided-CoT template, part of the improvement could stem from the structured prompting itself rather than retrieved domain knowledge. This is the single most important evidence gap for the paper's central claim.

The comparison to Watch & Learn (+2.2% on Jedi) versus GUIDE (+4.47% on AgentS3) is across different agents and baselines and is not a controlled comparison; framing this as 'outperforming by a large margin' overstates the evidence. Abstract claims 'over 5%' improvements while contributions and results report 4.5-7.5%—inconsistent and slightly inflated framing.

Grounding knowledge, one of two headline contributions, adds only +0.69-0.80% overall over planning alone, and in some domains hurts (Qwen3-VL Chrome drops from 41.22 to 36.87 when full dual-channel is used); the dual-channel story is weaker than the framing suggests.

Reproducibility concerns: the system depends on live YouTube availability, auto-generated subtitles, and closed-source APIs (GPT-5.1, GPT-4.1, Seed-1.8), making exact replication impossible; no code release is mentioned. Statistical significance/variance across OSWorld runs (which are noisy, especially with temperature 1.0 and stochastic API outputs) is never reported, and gains of +0.7-0.8pp are within plausible run-to-run variance.

Annotator ablation (Tab. 2b) contains an unexplained anomaly: Seed-1.8 outperforms GPT-5.1 as annotator despite being the smaller model, while the default pipeline uses GPT-5.1; the per-domain ablation (Tab. 3) rests on only 50 tasks with as few as 1 task per domain (OS), making per-domain conclusions unreliable.

Inference-time costs beyond API spend are non-trivial: per-task video retrieval and download, annotation latency, and +2.1s per-step overhead; the practicality of 'real-time' retrieval before task execution (video download + Whisper + 30 frame-pair GPT-5.1 calls) is not analyzed against task time budgets.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper decomposes GUI agent 'domain bias' into planning-level and grounding-level failures, and this taxonomy is carried consistently through the method design (dual-channel knowledge injection) and the analysis.

Meaningful technical distinction from prior work: unlike Watch & Learn and other video-based GUI approaches that rely on pre-built or manually curated corpora, GUIDE performs live web retrieval per task via a three-stage subtitle-driven Video-RAG pipeline, which is a practical and scalable capability.

Strong and broad empirical evidence: consistent 4.5-7.5% gains on the full OSWorld benchmark across three agent architectures (open-source 8B, closed-source, multi-agent), with per-domain breakdowns, knowledge-channel ablations, grounding-element-count ablations, and annotation-model ablations.

Unusually thorough pipeline-level evaluation: human studies of domain classification (100% precision, F1=95.27), topic extraction (96% acceptable), and the Meaningful filter (P=96.0, R=91.6 on 4,500 frames), plus a detailed cost accounting (Tables 5-7) that quantifies the full API spend (~$114.6 for the benchmark).

Honest failure analysis: Appendix F explicitly characterizes two failure modes (planning mismatch and grounding mismatch) with concrete examples and motivates mitigations, rather than hiding negative cases.
Genuinely plug-and-play design: knowledge is natural-language only, requiring no parameter or architecture modification, which increases practical impact and adoptability.
The paper is well written and clearly organized, with sufficient implementation detail (full prompts in Appendix A, configuration in Appendix B) to support reproducibility of the pipeline design.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on proprietary frontier models: the annotation pipeline uses GPT-5.1, GPT-4.1, and GPT-4.1-mini, and the multi-agent evaluation uses a GPT-5.2 Worker. This weakens reproducibility, raises cost/availability concerns beyond the reported one-off API cost, and makes it hard to separate the contribution of GUIDE's pipeline design from the raw capability of the underlying annotator models.

Single-benchmark evaluation: all conclusions rest on OSWorld. OSWorld tasks involve widely used applications (GIMP, LibreOffice, VLC) with abundant tutorial coverage-82.8% retrieval coverage confirms this-which is arguably a best-case scenario; generalization to niche, internal, or enterprise software with scarce web tutorials is not tested and is a significant limitation for the claimed real-world relevance.

The comparison with Watch & Learn is not apples-to-apples: the +2.2% baseline gain is measured on a different agent (Jedi) with an offline corpus, while GUIDE's gain is on a different, stronger baseline (AgentS3). Claims that GUIDE 'outperforms' Watch & Learn by a large margin should be softened, since the setups differ in agent, baseline, and retrieval source.

Statistical rigor is limited: no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the OSWorld gains. The grounding ablation (Table 2a) and per-domain ablation (Table 3) use only a 50-task subset, where individual domains have as few as 1 task (OS), making per-domain claims unreliable and the non-monotonic k trend (peak at k=5, +11.99pp) hard to interpret.

The annotation-model ablation (Table 2b) is puzzling: Seed-1.8 is both the executing agent and the best annotator (57.8% vs. 53.8% for GPT-5.1), raising questions about self-annotation effects and whether the annotator ranking is robust; this anomaly deserves analysis rather than just reporting the stronger-annotator-is-better trend that Seed-1.8 actually contradicts.

Live YouTube retrieval introduces reproducibility and provenance concerns: retrieved videos change over time, YouTube access via yt-dlp may violate platform terms of service, and copyright status of using tutorial content (including auto-generated captions) as training/inference material is not discussed. There is also a potential contamination concern: if tutorial videos covering the exact OSWorld tasks exist, the benchmark partially reduces to a retrieval-memory test rather than a general capability test.

Some gains are small and configuration-sensitive: grounding alone adds only +0.69-0.80% overall (and Multi-apps even declines from 26.88 to 25.74 on Seed-1.8), so the practical value of the grounding channel beyond complex-UI domains is modest relative to pipeline complexity.

Latency overhead is acknowledged (+2.1s per step) but the total inference-time cost of the retrieval-plus-annotation pipeline (per-task wall-clock) is not reported, which matters for the 'real-time' claim in the title.

strengths: The core idea—live retrieval of web tutorial videos at test time and converting them into structured, coordinate-free planning/grounding knowledge—is well-motivated and clearly differentiated from prior work (Watch & Learn, TongUI, VideoAgentTrek, Mobile-Agent-V), which either uses fixed corpora or manual video assignment.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for an agentic-systems paper: three agent architectures (single-model and multi-agent), cross-benchmark transfer to WindowsAgentArena without tuning, a same-backbone Watch & Learn-style raw-trajectory control that usefully isolates the contribution of structured decomposition, annotation-pipeline ablations (subtitle-only, no-OmniParser, annotator model, K, element count k), human audits of retrieval and filtering quality (Figs. 5, Tab. 8), a detailed cost analysis (Tabs. 9–11), and transparent failure-case analysis (Figs. 7–8).

The paper is honest about limitations: it reports the modest gain from grounding alone (+0.41pp), the sub-54% recall of the Meaningful filter on idle frames, latency overhead, and knowledge-injection-induced failures, and frames OmniParser as complementary rather than decisive under strong annotators.

The dual planning/grounding decomposition of 'domain bias' is a clean conceptual framing that matches the per-domain results (largest gains in Writer, Calc, GIMP) and the ablation attribution (planning carries ~86% of the gain), which strengthens the internal consistency of the story.
The knowledge format is agent-agnostic and training-free, and the supplementary prompt structures support reproducibility; code, dataset, and prompts are stated to be released.
weaknesses: Dependence on frontier proprietary models: the pipeline uses GPT-5.1 for annotation/decomposition and GPT-4.1 for retrieval, and the strongest evaluated agents rely on Seed-1.8/GPT-5.2 APIs. It is unclear how much of the gain comes from GUIDE's design versus the strength of these annotators; the authors themselves note the OmniParser contribution shrinks under a strong annotator. Ablation Tab. 7(b) helps, but the external validity for open-weight-only deployments is limited.

No statistical repetition on the full benchmark: the full OSWorld runs appear to be single runs (361 tasks), with seed repetition only on the 120-task ablation subset. Given gains of +4.47–7.48pp on ~361 tasks and stochastic agentic execution (plus the acknowledged Seed-1.8 malformed-output and Chrome network issues), confidence intervals are not reported; the Qwen3-VL-8B baseline is also taken from a prior report rather than reproduced, and its per-domain baseline is missing (Tab. 3).

Test-time live YouTube retrieval introduces non-determinism, availability risk, and potential copyright/redistribution concerns for videos, none of which are discussed; the paper also does not report how often retrieval fails or changes between benchmark runs.

Some parts of the gain likely stem from prompt engineering rather than retrieved knowledge per se: Mode B uses a structured guided-CoT template only when knowledge is injected; there is no control with an equal-length generic external-knowledge prompt or template without video content, so the injection-vs-template attribution is incomplete (the W&L-ICL control mitigates but does not fully resolve this).

Minor inconsistencies and presentation issues: k=7 stated in Sec. 4.1 vs k=5 in the Tab. 1 AgentS3 footnote; Tab. 5 contains anomalous values (VLC K=1 = 58.13 with only 5 tasks, VSCode 0.00 across all K); Table 3's W&L control is below the no-annotation baseline, which the paper interprets favorably but could also indicate an unfairly weak control configuration. Several per-domain ablation results are non-monotonic and small-sample (1 task for OS), making fine-grained claims fragile.

The contribution is primarily a systems/engineering integration of existing components (yt-dlp, Whisper, MOG2, OmniParser, LLM/VLM prompting) rather than a new algorithmic technique; as an Applied/Systems contribution this is acceptable, but the methodological novelty (three-stage subtitle filtering, pairwise VLM annotation) is incremental relative to VideoAgentTrek/Watch & Learn.

strengths: The framework is well-motivated: the planning-level vs. grounding-level decomposition of GUI 'domain bias' is a clean framing, and injecting natural-language, coordinate-free knowledge from tutorial videos is a sensible training-free mechanism for test-time adaptation.

The experimental effort is unusually thorough for this type of system paper: full OSWorld (361 tasks) across three agent architectures, cross-benchmark transfer to WindowsAgentArena, a same-backbone Watch & Learn-style raw-trajectory control that usefully isolates the value of structured decomposition (31.96 vs. 39.73), annotation-pipeline ablations with repeated seeds (Tab. 4), retrieval controls (Tab. 6), human audits of retrieval and the Meaningful filter, cost accounting, and honest failure-case analysis.

The paper is transparent about confounds (Seed-1.8 API parsing issues, Chrome network problems) and frames the knowledge as 'reference, not directive,' which addresses some concerns about misleading injections.
The retrieval ablation (Tab. 6) and the human evaluation of Stage 1/Stage 2 (Fig. 5) provide reasonable evidence that the subtitle-driven pipeline adds value beyond the candidate pool.
weaknesses: Limited scientific novelty. The core idea—retrieve tutorial videos and convert them into agent context—is a composition of known techniques (yt-dlp search, Whisper ASR, OmniParser, LLM/VLM prompting, prompt injection). The 'three-stage subtitle-driven retrieval' is essentially three LLM calls with hand-designed prompts, and the 'dual-anchored prompt' (repeating TOPIC at both ends of the context window) is prompt engineering rather than a principled method. Relative to Watch and Learn, TongUI, RAG-GUI, and OS-Symphony, the delta is primarily live retrieval and a different output format.

Heavy dependence on closed-source frontier models (GPT-5.1 annotator, GPT-4.1 retrieval, GPT-5.2 Worker, Seed-1.8) makes the contribution hard to attribute: it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the GUIDE framework versus the exceptional quality of the annotator LLM. The ablation in Tab. 7(b) shows even a much weaker annotator (GPT-4.1-mini) retains most of the gain, which paradoxically undercuts the paper's own claim that OmniParser/VLM pairwise annotation is a 'key innovation' (Tab. 4 shows OmniParser adds only +1.59pp).

Reproducibility and evaluation hygiene concerns. The pipeline performs live YouTube retrieval at test time using the OSWorld task instructions; retrieved videos may effectively be step-by-step solutions to benchmark tasks, which blurs the line between 'domain knowledge' and direct task hints. YouTube content also changes over time, so results are not reliably re-runnable. Additionally, the Qwen3-VL-8B baseline is taken from another paper's report (Tab. 1†) rather than re-run, and no variance/significance estimates are given for the full 361-task runs (seeds only for the 120-task ablation), although run-to-run variance on OSWorld is nontrivial relative to the +4.47pp smallest claimed gain.

The dual-channel story is weaker than advertised: grounding contributes only +0.41–0.80pp (and can even hurt: overall planning+grounding gains are smaller than planning-only on several domains, e.g., Multi 27.89→25.74 for Seed-1.8, and the W&L control shows grounding-only near baseline). The paper's second 'key innovation' therefore accounts for ~10–15% of the benefit in most settings.

Some reported numbers invite skepticism: Tab. 5 shows VLC collapsing from 58.13 (K=1) to 20.00 (K=2) and impress 33.33→50.34 (a non-terminating decimal for n=6 tasks is arithmetically impossible on a per-task 0/1 scale), suggesting reporting errors or aggregation inconsistencies that reduce confidence in the tables.

Cost/latency accounting exists but the practical deployment story is thin: +2.1s per-step latency, retrieval failure on 17% of tasks, and two acknowledged systematic failure modes (planning mismatch, grounding mismatch) with only proposed—not implemented—mitigations.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the decomposition of GUI-agent 'domain bias' into planning-level and grounding-level failure modes is crisp, and the dual-channel knowledge design directly targets each manifestation. This conceptual framing is a genuine contribution beyond the pipeline itself.

Novel and practical capability: GUIDE is, to my knowledge, the first system to retrieve and process raw tutorial videos from the open web (YouTube) at test time, rather than relying on pre-built corpora or manually assigned demo videos. The distinction from Watch & Learn, TongUI, and VideoAgentTrek is clearly articulated.

Comprehensive and well-designed empirical evidence: full 361-task OSWorld evaluation across three agent architectures (single-model and multi-agent), cross-benchmark transfer to WindowsAgentArena (+10.21/+12.46pp), a same-backbone Watch & Learn-style raw-trajectory control (which scores *below* baseline, convincingly isolating the structured knowledge decomposition as the source of gains), annotation-pipeline ablations with repeated seeds, retrieval-matching controls with human annotation, and an unusually thorough human audit of the Meaningful filter (4,500 frames, 3 annotators) and retrieval quality.

Honest and transparent reporting: the paper discusses increased per-step latency, the ~17% of tasks that receive no injected knowledge, non-monotonic K behavior, modest OmniParser contribution, and includes a detailed failure-case analysis with concrete derailing examples. The cost analysis (App. E) is exemplary for reproducibility and practicality assessment.

Strong practical significance: training-free, plug-and-play, architecture-agnostic, with per-task cost under $0.27 — an attractive alternative to manual annotation and fine-tuning for keeping GUI agents current with evolving software.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on frontier proprietary models: GPT-5.1 performs the frame-pair annotation and knowledge decomposition, GPT-5.2 and GPT-4.1 the retrieval and multi-agent roles. The paper does not adequately address (i) reproducibility given API churn, and (ii) whether the annotated knowledge could constitute an implicit distillation channel for the very models being evaluated (e.g., AgentS3's GPT-5.2 Worker receiving knowledge produced by GPT-5.1). A smaller-annotator ablation exists (Tab. 7b) but only on a 50-task subset.

Main results lack variance/significance reporting: the full-benchmark runs (Tab. 1-3) appear to be single runs, while repeated seeds appear only in the 120-task subset ablation. Given gains of +0.69-0.80pp attributed to grounding, and known environment/network noise in OSWorld (which the authors themselves acknowledge in 'Practical Notes'), significance of the smaller deltas is unclear. The multi-apps domain actually *degrades* under dual-channel injection on Seed-1.8 (26.88 -> 25.74), which deserves discussion.

The improvement of the Watch & Learn-style control (31.96 vs. 33.90 baseline) may partly reflect suboptimal ICL implementation rather than a fundamental superiority of GUIDE's decomposition; a stronger raw-trajectory baseline (e.g., retrieval of well-matched demo clips as images) would strengthen the attribution claim.

Retrieval is per-task and uses the exact task instruction, making GUIDE effectively a form of test-time adaptation tailored to the benchmark's task distribution. Ablations probe components, but there is no evaluation on genuinely held-out, post-hoc tasks to demonstrate that the acquired knowledge generalizes beyond instructions that directly shaped retrieval queries.

Presentation issues: the project-page URL in the abstract is empty; GPT-5.2/GPT-5.1/Seed-1.8 citations point to preprints/model cards of questionable public verifiability, which complicates exact replication; the '100% precision' claim in Fig. 5a rests on a 300-video sample and should be softened.

The claimed two 'key innovations' (subtitle-driven staged retrieval; pairwise VLM annotation) are engineering-heavy compositions of existing tools (yt-dlp, Whisper, MOG2, OmniParser, LLM prompting). The novelty is in the system design and the demonstrated effectiveness rather than algorithmic depth, which some reviewers may weigh against it — though for an Applied/Systems contribution this is acceptable.
